turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry we're late, doctor. The bus was a pure disaster and then there wasn't a space in the car park. I'm all over the place already.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're grand. Sit in, no rush on my side.
[SEG0003] person_3 (NURSE): I'll grab the observations while ye settle. Sleeve up for me.
[SEG0004] person_3 (NURSE): Blood pressure is 128 over 78, pulse 92, temperature 37.1, and the oxygen is 98 percent.
[SEG0005] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Parking aside, what has you in.
[SEG0006] person_1 (PATIENT): It's the eyes. They've gone yellow, and the pee is dark like tea, and I'm wrecked tired. I can't get it out of my head.
[SEG0007] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yellow eyes, dark urine, and the tiredness. When did the colour start.
[SEG0008] person_1 (PATIENT): Umm, about four days. We got home Monday and I saw it Tuesday in the mirror, or was it Wednesday, no, four days, I'm sure of that.
[SEG0009] person_4 (CAREGIVER): Tuesday, yeah. I seen the yellow when he was making the tea, and the urine was near black. He was pacing half the night, worried sick.
[SEG0010] person_1 (PATIENT): Is it the liver? A lad on the tour said his uncle went yellow and was weeks in hospital. Am I going in. Tell me straight.

[SEG0011] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thinking out loud, so stop me if I rush. Yellow in the whites means bilirubin is up, so the liver or the bile pipes are involved. It does not mean hospital today. Bloods first, then I'll know how cross the liver is.
[SEG0012] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm. The tiredness, I'm sleeping half the afternoon and I'm still wrecked. Is that part of the same thing.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): It often comes with it. Any pain in the tummy, or any vomiting.
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No vomiting. There's a dull ache under the right ribs, not terrible, more a niggle, comes and goes. And the poo has gone pale, like clay.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pale stool fits the same picture. Any fever, shakes, or itching.
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No fever. No shakes. The arms are a bit itchy at night. Does itching mean it's worse, because I keep frightening myself reading.
[SEG0017] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He was scratching in the chair, and he barely touched the dinner. I live in with him, I'm his carer, so I see what he eats.
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): I wasn't hungry. The smell of the food turned my stomach. Should I be forcing myself to eat.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't force a big feed. Small amounts will do. Now, the trip and the stalls.
[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Bus tour in Portugal. Roadside stalls, seafood and salad that looked dodgy. A few of the others came down with a vomiting bug. I didn't, I just went yellow.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any cough, or trouble breathing.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No. The chest is grand, breathing is fine. Is it the lungs as well now.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): No, I'm only making sure there's not a second thing going on. What about alcohol, on the holiday or at home.
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No. I don't drink. Not a drop on the trip, and I never have. My dad was a fierce drinker so I swore off it.
[SEG0025] person_4 (CAREGIVER): His mam is on the metformin for her sugar, diabetes. She keeps ringing, thinking it's her tablets. He doesn't take any of hers.
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): A thousand milligrams she takes, that's her affair. Doctor, err, is this hepatitus from the food. I googled at two in the morning and I'm really scared.

[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Hepatitis A is what I'm leaning towards. Roadside food, others on the tour unwell, then the jaundice. I'm not calling it definite. Another hepatitis is possible, and a bile duct stone is less likely but not gone.
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): A stone, though? Would the pain not be desperate. And can I pass it to my sister, she brings the baby over. What do I do in the house.

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stone pain is usually much sharper, so the niggle argues against it, but I want the bloods before I drop it. If it is hep A it goes hand to mouth, so wash up, your own towel, no sharing cups.
[SEG0030] person_4 (CAREGIVER): He took stuff on the holiday too. Crocin from the chemist over there, for a headache. Two of an evening.
[SEG0031] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah, Crocin. Same as paracetemol, I think. Two a night for three nights, then I stopped once the pee went dark. Did I wreck the liver doing that.
[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): A few nights of normal paracetamol would not cause this, and stopping was fair. Anything else you take, and any drug allergies?

[SEG0033] person_1 (PATIENT): No allergies, nothing I know of. I take the water tablet every morning, the little white one, two and a half milligrams, for the blood pressure. Been on it for years. I don't miss it.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Two and a half milligrams is bendroflumethiazide. Stay on it, don't stop, it isn't behind this.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Is bendroflumethazide bad for the liver all the same. And is there a diet, and can I have coffee. Sorry, the questions won't stop.

[SEG0036] person_2 (DOCTOR): Not at that dose. Eat little and often, whatever sits well, plenty of water, and coffee is fine. Rest up, no heavy work this week, and stay off the drink, which you already are.
[SEG0037] person_3 (NURSE): Hands are a bit clammy. Pulse is regular. Will I line up the bloods before ye go.

[SEG0038] person_2 (DOCTOR): Yes, get the bloods today. Lie back and lift the shirt. Whites of the eyes are yellow, the tummy is soft and tender under the right ribs, I can just feel the liver edge, and there's no guarding.
[SEG0039] person_1 (PATIENT): You can feel the liver? Is it swollen. I'm a porter in the hotel, how long am I going to be off. This is a lot.
[SEG0040] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mildly enlarged, which fits inflammation rather than anything dramatic. Light duties if the hotel can sort it. I won't promise a timeline until the numbers are in.

[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Here's the plan. Liver blood tests today, the full panel, and hepatitis serology for A, B and C. If the bloods point to a blockage I'll add an ultrasound, but I'm not booking the scan today.
[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Are the results today. What if they're terrible. Do I come back, and should the rest of the tour get checked. I'm going to stew.

[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): The liver numbers are often back this evening or tomorrow, and the serology takes a few days. I want you back in clinic in one week regardless. Ring sooner if you're more yellow, if you start vomiting, or if you're confused or very drowsy.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): Can I ring as well if the itch gets bad, before the week is up. And the bloods, it's a needle isn't it. I hate needles.
[SEG0045] person_3 (NURSE): It is one needle in the arm, and I'll take you out for it now. Quick as I can.
[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ring about the itch too, don't sit frightened. We'll go through every result when I see you in the week.

spec.situation: Person with yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness after eating at roadside stalls on a trip; others at the trip also ill; alcohol denied; liver blood tests and hepatitis serology planned.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

bad.reason: Food smell turned his stomach supports nausea, but temporality 'current' is not explicitly stated.
bad.text: nausea (category=gastrointestinal, status=present, temporality=current, aggravating_factors=smell of food, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Doctor advised own towel and no sharing cups, plus 'wash up' not specifically wash hands.
bad.text: Wash hands, use own towel, and do not share cups (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

bad.reason: Doctor says ring sooner for more yellow, vomiting, confused, very drowsy, or itch; 'gets worse' not stated.
bad.text: Ring sooner if more yellow, vomiting, confused, drowsy, or the itch gets worse (action_type=counselling, status=recommended, responsible_person=patient)

omissions.text: Dark urine was described as starting with the jaundice about 4 days ago, with caregiver noting it was 'near black'.
Denied abdominal pain and vomiting was asked incorrectly in the recorded facts: the patient denied vomiting, but did report a dull intermittent ache under the right ribs.
Negative respiratory review included both no cough and no trouble breathing.
Travel/exposure history: recent bus tour in Portugal with roadside stalls; ate seafood and salad that looked dodgy; several others on the tour developed a vomiting bug.
Paracetamol/Crocin use was clarified as 'two each evening' for headache, then stopped once urine went dark.
Hepatitis serology was specified as testing for hepatitis A, B and C.
Results timing was discussed: liver blood results likely back this evening or tomorrow; serology takes a few days.
